cards.question: At the inguinal level, what is the order of structures from lateral to medial?
cards.answer: NAVeL: femoral Nerve — femoral Artery — femoral Vein — empty space — Lymphatics (within femoral canal). The artery lies at the mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis); the nerve sits ~1 cm lateral, separated from the artery by the iliopectineal arch — relevant for femoral nerve block needle placement.

cards.question: What does a femoral nerve block cover, and what does it miss?
cards.answer: It covers the anterior thigh (skin and quadriceps), medial leg (saphenous nerve below the knee) and periosteum of the femur — sufficient for analgesia after femoral neck or shaft fracture and for knee surgery in combination with a sciatic block. It misses the posterior-thigh skin (principally posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, S1–S3; distinct from sciatic motor supply to posterior-thigh muscles), hip joint (obturator + sciatic + femoral all contribute), and lateral thigh (lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh).

cards.question: Where does the sciatic nerve divide and why does that matter for popliteal block?
cards.answer: The sciatic typically divides into tibial and common peroneal branches in the popliteal fossa, ~7 cm proximal to the popliteal crease. Ultrasound-guided popliteal block targets the nerve just proximal to the bifurcation so one injection captures both branches — block below the bifurcation may spare one division and leave one division unblocked. The lateral border of the foot is sural territory, with variable tibial/common fibular contributions; most dorsum is superficial fibular/peroneal and the first web space deep fibular. An isolated peroneal block cannot be assumed to cover the lateral border.
